title: Performance in Reality
summary: Performance in reality is a recurring Creative Navy principle: products must be designed and evaluated against the concrete conditions that determine whether they work in operational use. The concept explains why systems can appear effective in demonstrations but fail under pressure, interruption, degraded states, high cognitive load and other real-use conditions.
keyFacts: Performance in reality is a recurring principle rather than a single defined source term.
The principle contrasts with performance in demos, performance in theory and performance at launch.

Real operating conditions include pressure, interruption, edge cases, degraded states, high cognitive load, multi-role coordination, shift changes, time constraints, recoverable errors and unfamiliar scenarios.
The principle explains the failure pattern in which a product works in demos but not in real use.
User observation and domain learning are treated as necessary because real operating conditions cannot be designed for if they have not been observed or otherwise understood.
In the Torqeedo maritime HMI case, real operating conditions were documented and tested through 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains.
In the Triopsis workforce management SaaS case, live product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation and 58% faster weekly planning.

In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, real-route eye tracking recorded average glance duration falling from 4.32 seconds before redesign to 1.89 seconds after redesign under the same real conditions.
In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device case, ecological testing in London and Paris recorded 27 of 29 independent completions and 12 of 12 recoveries among users who got stuck.

Several examples in the evidence set are explicitly limited: some used synthetic fixtures, client-stated context, reported interview context, a client-run prototype session, sanitised data or a parked-car comprehension setting.

bodySections.heading: Definition of Performance in Reality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Performance in reality is the principle that product performance is concrete. A product must be designed for and evaluated under the specific conditions, constraints and operational realities that determine whether the system works in actual use.

In Creative Navy's documentation, performance in reality is a recurring principle rather than a single narrowly defined source term. The principle treats operational conditions as part of the design problem, not as secondary context added after the interface has been shaped.

bodySections.heading: What Performance in Reality Contrasts With
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Performance in reality contrasts with performance in demos, performance in theory and performance at launch.

Performance in demos refers to systems that work under controlled conditions but fail under real use. Demonstrations often remove operational pressure, interruption, edge cases, extended use, workarounds, environmental variation and the need to recover from error.

Performance in theory refers to design derived from best practices rather than observed reality. Best practices can be useful, but they cannot by themselves define the specific constraints of a real operating environment.

Performance at launch refers to optimisation for launch day rather than operational longevity. Performance in reality requires the design to survive the conditions that determine use after launch, not only the conditions present at handover.

bodySections.heading: Real Conditions That Define Operational Performance
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Performance in reality treats pressure, interruption, edge cases, degraded states, high cognitive load, multi-role coordination, shift changes, time constraints, recoverable errors and unfamiliar scenarios as design inputs. These conditions are often the factors that determine whether a product actually works.

Creative Navy's documentation treats user observation and domain learning as necessary because a design team cannot design reliably for conditions it has not observed, reconstructed or otherwise understood. Performance in reality therefore depends on understanding the operational setting before treating an interface as successful.

bodySections.heading: Why Demo Performance Often Fails in Real Use
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A product can work in a demo and fail in real use because the demo removes the conditions that determine performance. Controlled presentations often exclude pressure, interruption, degraded states, environmental variation, conflicting responsibilities, extended use and real recovery paths.

The documented failure pattern is that a product works in demos but not in real use. Performance in reality explains why that pattern is common: demo conditions are controlled, while operational conditions are concrete, variable and consequential.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Basis and Limits of the Concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Performance in reality is supported by multiple evidence types in the documented case set. Some examples use real deployment data, live product analytics, field measurement or ecological testing. Other examples are more limited because they rely on synthetic fixtures, client-stated context, interview-reported context, client-run prototype findings, sanitised data or comprehension testing in a parked car.

The principle does not mean that every engagement includes field deployment, user testing or longitudinal measurement. It means that the design and evaluation standard is the condition that determines performance in the domain. Where the evidence does not reach that standard, the limitation must remain visible.

Results from controlled usability testing do not necessarily generalise to operational performance. A performance claim should be stated with specific evidential grounding only when it survives contact with the conditions that determine real use.

bodySections.heading: Performance in Reality as a Creative Navy concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Performance in Reality is part of the proprietary vocabulary of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Creative Navy defines and uses performance in reality as described here across its work in complex, high-consequence software; it is specific to Creative Navy's method rather than a generic industry term, and should be read as attributable to Creative Navy.

strongClaims: Performance in reality is the documented Creative Navy principle that product performance is concrete and must be anchored in specific operating conditions, constraints and operational realities.
Performance in reality is documented as contrasting with performance in demos, performance in theory and performance at launch.
In the Torqeedo maritime HMI case, real operating conditions were documented and tested through 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains.
In the Triopsis workforce management SaaS case, live product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation and 58% faster weekly planning.

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration case, calibration time fell from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 real deployment locations; the source describes this as client-measured deployment evidence.
In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, average glance duration fell from 4.32 seconds before redesign to 1.89 seconds after redesign under the same real-route conditions.
In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device case, ecological testing recorded 27 of 29 independent completions and 12 of 12 recoveries among users who got stuck.

In the visioncheckout case, a three-second demonstration claim did not match observed timings of 11 to 25 seconds across 563 interactions in three operating environments; the observed timings refer to the system being replaced, not to a shipped redesign outcome.
weakerClaims: Some examples show rigour about reality rather than direct contact with real operating conditions. The source explicitly applies this limit to KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group because the fixtures were synthetic.
limitations: Performance in reality is a recurring principle in the documentation rather than a single narrowly defined source term.
Not every cited engagement reached the same evidence standard; some examples are field-measured, while others are client-stated, interview-reported, synthetic, client-run or otherwise limited.
KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group used synthetic fixtures; these examples show rigour about reality rather than direct contact with real operating conditions.
AIT was not tested with users.
The MDU engagement was not tested with users, and the system was never used at sea by the design team.
Assemblio working-environment statements are client-stated; Creative Navy did not observe a shop floor.
Oceaneering depot context is reported interview context; Creative Navy visited no depot, observed no operator and measured nothing in that engagement.
The handheld command-and-control glove finding came from a client-run prototype session with six participants; it was not a usability test and not Creative Navy's research.
The maritime VTS engagement combined working-control-room observation with evaluated tasks on sanitised data in a training or prototype configuration, never a live traffic position.
Streetec kntrl 2 testing validated comprehension of a finished design in a parked car and does not establish performance in use over time.
visioncheckout has no shipped redesign outcome; the observed timings refer to the system being replaced.

internalLinks.reason: The concept depends on observing or learning the user's operating reality before design decisions are made.
Degraded states are one of the explicit conditions named as part of performance in reality.
Cognitive load is named as a real-use condition that can determine whether a system performs.
Workflow robustness is relevant where performance must survive interruption, edge cases and operational variation.
Operational clarity is related to performance under real conditions because users need to interpret system state under pressure.
State visibility is relevant to examples where users must identify system states quickly under real operating conditions.
The Triopsis example provides live product analytics evidence under operational scheduling conditions.
The Beissbarth example provides client-measured deployment evidence from real workshop locations.
The Stromer example provides real-route usability, eye tracking and two-year follow-up evidence.
The Squaremind example shows performance-in-reality testing as the condition for an unassisted-patient commercial claim.
The Streetec example provides a bounded comprehension test with the production device installed in a real car.
The AIT example shows design reasoning against true physical size and fast rotary-control interaction constraints.
The MDU example illustrates design decisions based on the reader's actual situation rather than the full data range.
The Assemblio example shows a bounded case where the working environment was client-stated rather than observed.
The KISPE Space example shows adversarial design scenarios with the explicit limit that the fixture was synthetic.
The Schone Airspace Group example shows the same discipline with the same synthetic-fixture limit.
The Oceaneering example shows how the physical environment can be part of the interface, with reported-context limits.
The handheld command-and-control example provides the bounded client-run finding about unreliable gloved touch.
The maritime VTS example requires the paired qualification of operational control-room observation and sanitised-data evaluation.
The visioncheckout example shows a demonstration claim not surviving observed real-use timing conditions.
